label: Ancient Korea
pitch:
Three rival kingdoms fought for the Korean peninsula across seven centuries: Goguryeo Founded in the mountainous north, Baekje Founded in the fertile southwest, and Silla Founded in the southeast. When Gwanggaeto the Great expanded Goguryeo to its greatest extent and Goguryeo Defeats Sui China humiliated a million-man invasion, the world learned not to underestimate Korean warriors.

🔑 Key Facts:
• Buddhism Arrives in Goguryeo in 372 CE transformed Korean spiritual life and sparked centuries of temple building
• Queen Seondeok of Silla became Korea's first female ruler and commissioned the Cheomseongdae Observatory, the oldest surviving observatory in East Asia
• General Kim Yu-sin led the campaigns that achieved Silla Unifies Korea in 668 CE
• Gaya Iron Trade made the southern confederacy a major exporter to China and Japan

🤔 Why It Matters: The unification forged a shared Korean identity that survived Mongol invasions, Japanese colonization, and modern division into North and South Korea — one of the longest continuous cultural traditions on Earth.

🎲 Wild Card: The Ondol Underfloor Heating system invented by Goguryeo channeled hot air beneath stone floors — and Koreans still use heated floors in their homes today, 1,800 years later.

spans.label: Gojoseon
spans.description: Korea's legendary first kingdom, traditionally founded by Dangun in 2333 BCE. Gojoseon grew from a Bronze Age chiefdom into a powerful state that controlled trade between China and the Korean peninsula before falling to Han dynasty invasion in 108 BCE.

spans.label: Han Commanderies
spans.description: After conquering Gojoseon, the Han dynasty established four commanderies on the northern peninsula. Lelang, the longest-lasting, became a conduit for Chinese culture, technology, and trade goods flowing into Korea for over four centuries.

spans.label: Proto-Three Kingdoms
spans.description: Small tribal states and walled-town polities competed across the Korean peninsula. Silla, Goguryeo, and Baekje were founded during this period, laying the groundwork for the Three Kingdoms era.

spans.label: Goguryeo
spans.description: The largest and most militarily powerful of the Three Kingdoms, Goguryeo controlled Manchuria and northern Korea. It repelled massive Sui and Tang Chinese invasions and left a legacy of mountain fortresses and painted tomb murals.

spans.label: Baekje
spans.description: The southwestern kingdom was renowned for refined Buddhist art, maritime trade, and cultural diplomacy. Baekje transmitted Buddhism, writing, and advanced technology to Japan, profoundly shaping early Japanese civilization.

spans.label: Silla
spans.description: Starting as the smallest of the Three Kingdoms in the southeast, Silla developed the Hwarang warrior corps and spectacular gold-crown culture. It ultimately allied with Tang China to conquer Baekje and Goguryeo, unifying Korea.

spans.label: Gaya Confederacy
spans.description: A loose confederation of city-states in the southern Nakdong River basin, Gaya was the peninsula's leading iron producer. Its iron ingots were exported to China and Japan before Silla absorbed the last Gaya states.

spans.label: Unified Silla
spans.description: After expelling Tang forces from the peninsula, Silla ruled a unified Korea from its capital at Gyeongju. The period saw a golden age of Buddhist art, international trade, and cultural achievement before internal decay led to the rise of Later Three Kingdoms.

events.label: Dangun Founds Gojoseon
events.description: Korea's founding legend: the god-prince Hwanung weds a bear-turned-woman, and their son Dangun Wanggeom establishes Gojoseon, the peninsula's first kingdom. Traditionally dated to 2333 BCE, it's the cornerstone of Korean national identity.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The story survives only because a Buddhist monk, Iryeon (1206-1289 CE), wrote it down in the Samguk Yusa more than 3,500 years after the supposed event. Hwanung is said to have descended with three "heavenly seals" and three thousand followers, taking charge of wind, rain, and clouds. The October 3 holiday that celebrates the founding, Gaecheonjeol, doesn't actually mean "Foundation Day" but "the day the sky opened." And there's a quiet absurdity baked into the tale: the bear-woman Ungnyeo endured a 100-day trial but transformed after just 21 days, leaving the math forever a little off.

events.label: Korean Bronze Age Begins
events.description: Bronze-working seeped into Korea from Manchuria and northern China, but Korean smiths soon went their own way, turning out distinctive daggers, ritual mirrors, and bells used more for ceremony than for war.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The earliest signature weapon is the Liaoning-type dagger (also called lute- or pear-shaped) of roughly 1000-400 BCE, with a curvy blade and a telltale detachable handle, the feature that sets it apart from one-piece Chinese daggers. By the 5th-4th centuries BCE a sleeker, narrower "Korean-type" dagger had evolved out of it, paired with bronze mirrors covered in dense geometric line patterns so fine that recreating them today is genuinely hard. Both daggers and mirrors show up almost exclusively in elite graves, which is why archaeologists read them as badges of chiefly and ritual power rather than tools of everyday life.

events.label: Mumun Pottery Period
events.description: The long stretch (roughly 1500 to 300 BCE) named after plain, undecorated "Mumun" pottery that replaced the older comb-patterned ware. It's the era when Koreans settled into farming villages, built dolmens, and developed real social pecking orders.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The defining site is Songguk-ri in South Chungcheong Province, a Middle-to-Late Mumun village (about 850-300 BCE) packed with rice remains and irrigation canals, where archaeologists found the round pit-houses and bronze-dagger burials that gave a whole sub-culture its name. The word "mumun" literally means "no pattern," and the switch to plain pots wasn't about losing skill but about a new way of living. Far from primitive, these villagers were already digging storage pits and laying out their settlements with deliberate organization.

events.label: Rice Cultivation Arrives in Korea
events.description: Wet-rice farming, growing rice in flooded paddies, spread from China into the warm, wet south of the peninsula. It was a turning point: rice fed bigger populations, demanded teamwork, and helped harden Korea's social hierarchies.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Paddy farming is brutally communal: the fields have to be diked, leveled, flooded, and drained on one shared schedule, so dozens of families end up locked into cooperating over a single water source. Scattered rice grains turn up at central-western Korean sites dated to roughly 3000 BCE, but the real takeoff came in the Bronze Age, with actual paddy fields and irrigation channels excavated at Mumun villages. Some archaeologists even argue rice was at first a prestige food, a status grain for the powerful, before it became the everyday staple it is now.

events.label: Korean Dolmen Culture
events.description: Korea is the dolmen capital of the world: tens of thousands of these megalithic tombs (a giant flat capstone propped on upright stones) dot the peninsula. They mark the graves of Bronze Age chiefs powerful enough to command armies of laborers.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Estimates run past 35,000 surviving dolmens in Korea, around 40 percent of every dolmen on the planet. The three UNESCO sites, Gochang, Hwasun, and Ganghwa, were inscribed in 2000 and together hold over a thousand of them in one of the densest clusters anywhere. The biggest stones are monsters: a single Ganghwa capstone measures roughly 23 feet (7.1 meters) long and stands taller than a person, all of it hauled and hoisted by people who had no wheels, no draft animals, and no metal cranes.

events.label: Korean Shamanism (Muism)
events.description: Muism, Korea's homegrown shamanism, is older than every imported religion on the peninsula. Its mudang shamans, usually women, contact the spirit world through loud, theatrical rituals called gut, full of music, dance, and trance.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The very word "shaman" entered English in the late 1600s from the Tungusic languages of Siberia (from saman), and Korean shamanic vocabulary echoes those northern roots: "mudang" may trace back to terms for female shamans like the Buryat udagan and Evenki udugan, found in a band of related cultures stretching across Siberia. A gut isn't a private prayer but a communal performance, the shaman feeding, entertaining, and bargaining with the gods on the village's behalf. Even now anthropologists quietly debate whether "shaman" is the right label, since the Korean tradition has its own distinct flavor.

events.label: Iron Age Begins in Korea
events.description: Around 400 BCE iron-working spread into Korea from China through Manchuria, the same route bronze had taken earlier. Cheap, abundant iron tools and weapons reshaped farming and war and tilted power toward whoever controlled iron production.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Archaeologists treat the 4th century BCE as the start of Korea's Iron Age, with the stretch from roughly 300 to 100 BCE labeled the Early Iron Age. The earliest pieces were cast iron, a Chinese specialty made by melting iron fully liquid in a furnace, so any cast-iron find in Korea is taken as proof the technology arrived from China rather than being invented locally. The shift mattered fast: stronger blades and plows let chiefs concentrate wealth and people, setting up the bigger states to come.

events.label: Wiman Seizes Gojoseon Throne
events.description: Around 194 BCE Wiman, a refugee from the Chinese state of Yan, was handed border-guard duty by King Jun of Gojoseon, then turned his troops on his host and took the throne. The state he founded (Wiman Joseon) grew rich skimming the trade between Han China and the peninsula's peoples.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Wiman seems to have fled east in the chaos after the Yan king Lu Wan rebelled against the new Han dynasty and was defeated, around 195 BCE. The ousted King Jun didn't vanish quietly: he escaped south by sea and set himself up among the southern Korean polities, styling himself "King of Han" (the Korean Han, no relation to China's Han). Almost everything we know about this comes from one source, chapter 115 of Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, China's first great history, written about a century later.

events.label: Fall of Gojoseon
events.description: After Wiman Joseon blocked southern Koreans from trading directly with China, Emperor Wu of Han invaded in 109 BCE. A year of fighting ended in 108 BCE when insiders murdered the king and surrendered the capital, finishing off Korea's first kingdom.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The invasion was nearly a fiasco. The Han sent two forces who openly feuded: Yang Pu sailed a fleet across the Bohai Sea while Xun Zhi marched overland through Liaodong, and a reckless advance gutted Yang Pu's army down to about 7,000 men by the time it reached the capital, Wanggeom-seong. The king who held out was Ugeo, Wiman's grandson; he was assassinated in 108 BCE by his own surrendering officials, and a minister named Seong Gi who kept fighting was killed too. Emperor Wu was so unhappy with how it all went that he had both of his commanders punished.

events.label: Han Commanderies Established
events.description: With Gojoseon conquered, Han China carved its territory into four commanderies (colonial provinces run by Chinese officials): Lelang, Zhenfan, Lintun, and Xuantu. They piped Chinese culture and goods into Korea while stirring the resistance that helped native kingdoms form.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The whole arrangement was an extension of the Chinese state onto Korean soil, complete with Chinese governors, law, and tax collectors. It didn't hold together: three of the four were too far from China and too costly to garrison, and within roughly thirty years Zhenfan and Lintun were scrapped and Xuantu was pushed back into Manchuria. Our knowledge of these districts leans heavily on Chinese dynastic histories, since the commanderies left little that survived in Korean sources.

events.label: Samhan Confederacies Emerge
events.description: South of Chinese control, the peninsula's lower two-thirds organized into three loose confederacies the Chinese called the Samhan ("Three Han"): Mahan in the southwest, Jinhan in the southeast, and Byeonhan along the south-central coast. From them would grow Baekje, Silla, and the Gaya states.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: These weren't kingdoms but clusters of small walled-town communities, counted in Chinese records as about 54 in Mahan and roughly 12 each in Jinhan and Byeonhan, near 78 in all, with Jinhan alone holding an estimated 40,000 to 50,000 households. Our fullest portrait of them comes from the Sanguozhi (Records of the Three Kingdoms), a Chinese history compiled in the late 3rd century CE whose "Account of the Eastern Barbarians" describes the lands south of Lelang. As Chinese influence faded after the 2nd century CE, iron ingots circulated as money in the Jinhan and Byeonhan trade.

events.label: Lelang Commandery Flourishes
events.description: Once the other three commanderies folded, Lelang near modern Pyongyang stood alone as China's outpost in Korea. For four centuries it functioned as a working Chinese city, churning out lacquerware, bronze mirrors, and paperwork that rubbed off on the surrounding Korean polities.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Lelang's wealth is famous because of its tombs: Japanese-led digs around Pyongyang in the early 1900s pulled out fine Han lacquer bowls, bronze mirrors, and gold filigree. Some lacquers carry dated maker's inscriptions running from 85 BCE to 102 CE, and they were manufactured far away in Sichuan in western China, then shipped clear across the continent to this colony. Lelang outlasted the rest until 313 CE, when the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo, under King Micheon, finally swallowed it and ended Chinese rule on the peninsula.

events.label: Silla Founded
events.description: Tradition says the boy-king Hyeokgeose, hatched from an egg, was made ruler by six village clans in the Gyeongju basin, founding the kingdom that would outlast all its rivals.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Silla turned out to be one of the longest-lived dynasties anywhere on earth, running from its legendary 57 BCE founding to 935 CE — close to a thousand years. The crown didn't even stay in one family: the early kingdom was ruled in turn by the Park clan (Hyeokgeose's line), then the Seok clan, and finally the Gyeongju Kim clan, who held it for the rest of Silla's history. The kingdom's first name wasn't even Silla but 'Saro,' one of the small statelets clustered around the valley before they fused into one.

events.label: Goguryeo Founded
events.description: Jumong (later honored as King Dongmyeong), a divine archer born from an egg, fled jealous brothers and founded Goguryeo in the mountainous Yalu River country, the kingdom that would become the warrior state of the three.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: In the legend Jumong isn't a peasant adventurer but a runaway prince of Buyeo, an older kingdom up in Manchuria, who fled south after a power struggle with the other princes and set up shop in a region called Jolbon. 'Jumong' was reportedly Buyeo slang for a crack shot with a bow, which is why his name gets translated as 'skilled archer.' Goguryeo wasn't founded by one man and his followers alone either: it grew out of an alliance binding the Buyeo newcomers to five local clans already living along the river.

events.label: Baekje Founded
events.description: Onjo, said to be a son of Jumong, led followers south from the north and founded Baekje in the rich Han River basin, near what is now Seoul.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Onjo planted his first capital, Wiryeseong, on the Han River right inside modern Seoul — making the South Korean capital, in a sense, one of the oldest continuously important sites on the peninsula. Historians slice Baekje's whole 700-year run by which city was its capital: the long Hanseong period (18 BCE–475 CE), then Ungjin, then Sabi. That first chapter ended violently in 475, when Goguryeo troops stormed Hanseong and killed Baekje's King Gaero, forcing the survivors to flee south and start over.

events.label: Gaya Confederacy Formed
events.description: A loose confederacy of iron-rich city-states emerged in the southern Nakdong River basin, famous for its metalwork and its tight trade ties with Japan.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Gaya gets its own six-egg origin myth: a golden box wrapped in red silk supposedly drifted down from heaven onto a sacred peak near modern Gimhae, holding six eggs that hatched into six boys. The eldest, Suro, became king of the leading state, Geumgwan Gaya, while his 'brothers' founded the rest — a tidy story for why the confederacy was six kingdoms and never one. Suro's reign is dated to around 42 CE, and folklore even gives him a foreign bride, a princess said to have arrived by sea from a distant land called Ayuta, often linked (controversially) to India.

events.label: Gaya Iron Trade
events.description: The Gaya states, growing out of iron-rich Byeonhan, became the peninsula's iron powerhouse, shipping ingots and weapons across the sea and using standardized iron bars almost like coins.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Gaya's heart was Geumgwan Gaya around modern Gimhae, at the mouth of the Nakdong River near present-day Busan, a perfect spot for sea trade. Its iron and armor moved out to the Wa (the polities of early Japan), to the Lelang colony in the north, and to Baekje, and in return Gaya pulled in prestige goods like bronze mirrors and lacquerware. By the late 4th century the lower Nakdong was mass-producing iron ingots cut to standard weights and sizes, a step toward treating metal as true currency.

events.label: Ondol Underfloor Heating
events.description: Goguryeo perfected the ondol — a system that pipes hot air and smoke from an outdoor furnace through flues beneath a stone floor — giving Korea a heating method its people still build their homes around two thousand years later.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The word ondol literally means "warm stone," and the older Korean name gudeul comes from a phrase meaning "heated stone." It works on the same principle as the Roman hypocaust (the Romans' under-floor furnace heating), but Koreans appear to have been warming their floors at least a century earlier, with the simplest forms traced back toward 1000 BCE. Because the warmest spot in the house was the floor, Koreans took to sitting, eating, and sleeping low to the ground — a habit that still shapes Korean homes and explains the heated floors in modern apartments.

events.label: Goguryeo Mountain Fortresses
events.description: Goguryeo built a network of mountain fortresses — stone walls tracing the ridgelines of strategic peaks — designed to shelter whole populations during a siege and to choke off the passes any invader had to use.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Unlike Chinese fortifications built of brick, Goguryeo's castles were faced with stone over an earth-and-rubble core, a method so respected that even Chinese sources of the day praised the kingdom's fortress-building skill. The payoff came in 645, when Emperor Taizong of Tang threw an army said to number 200,000 against tiny Ansi Fortress, defended by only about 4,000 men. The defenders held through the summer, beating back siege towers with rock traps and fire until winter forced the world's mightiest army to give up and retreat — the mountain fortress doing exactly the job it was built for.

events.label: Goguryeo Conquers Lelang
events.description: Under King Micheon, Goguryeo seized Lelang Commandery, finally expelling the last Chinese administrative outpost from the Korean peninsula after some four centuries.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Goguryeo struck while China was busy falling apart — the Jin dynasty was disintegrating into civil war — and snapped up Lelang in 313, then the neighboring Daifang Commandery the very next year, clearing out the whole Chinese foothold in two quick strokes. The Chinese presence it ended had lasted roughly 400 years, dating back to the Han conquest of Gojoseon. From 313 onward the contest for the peninsula was strictly an inside job, fought among Goguryeo, Baekje, and Silla with no foreign administration left on the map.

events.label: Goguryeo Tomb Murals
events.description: Goguryeo nobles had themselves buried in stone chambers under earth mounds, the walls painted with vivid murals of hunts, dances, wrestling, and cosmic guardians — the closest thing we have to color photographs of life in an ancient Korean kingdom.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Roughly 120 of these mural tombs survive — about 80 in North Korea and 38 in China. The famous Anak Tomb No. 3 carries a dated inscription pinning it to 357 CE and naming its occupant Dong Shou, a refugee official from the Chinese state of Former Yan, which is why its portrait shows such Chinese-style robes. In 2004 the tombs were honored by UNESCO as two separate World Heritage sites in the same year — the North Korean cluster and the Chinese one — a split that mirrors the ongoing tug-of-war over whose history Goguryeo belongs to.

events.label: Buddhism Arrives in Goguryeo
events.description: The monk Sundo arrived from the Chinese state of Former Qin bearing scriptures and statues, making Goguryeo the first Korean kingdom to officially welcome Buddhism.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: This wasn't a wandering missionary but a diplomatic gift: the Former Qin ruler Fu Jian deliberately sent Sundo with texts and Buddhist images to the court of King Sosurim, religion arriving as a tool of statecraft between rulers. Sosurim grabbed the moment to overhaul his whole kingdom in a tight window — Buddhism in 372, a Confucian academy the same year, and a written legal code the next — converting a tribal federation into a centralized state almost on a schedule. Archaeology suggests Buddhist ideas had trickled into Goguryeo before 372; what changed that year was the state officially blessing them from the top down.

events.label: Taehak Confucian Academy
events.description: Goguryeo founded the Taehak, Korea's first state Confucian academy, to train the sons of the nobility in Chinese classics and the art of administration.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Taehak was set up under King Sosurim — the same king who accepted Buddhism that year — and it pointedly served the children of the aristocracy, making literacy and government office a privilege of birth rather than talent. It paired naturally with the written legal code Sosurim issued the very next year, in 373: together, school plus law book gave Goguryeo the two things a bureaucratic state can't run without, trained officials and rules they could apply. China itself took note of how thoroughly Goguryeo borrowed its institutional toolkit.

events.label: Goguryeo Legal Code
events.description: Goguryeo promulgated a formal legal code (yullyeong) in the same year it established the Taehak academy and received Buddhism — a triple modernization that transformed the kingdom from a tribal federation into a structured state with written laws, formal education, and state religion.

events.label: Buddhism Arrives in Baekje
events.description: In 384, the Indian monk Marananta sailed in from Eastern Jin China, and Baekje's King Chimnyu welcomed him into the palace and adopted Buddhism on the spot.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Chimnyu had been on the throne only months when Marananta arrived, and he died the very next year, in 385 — but not before ordering Korea's first Buddhist temple built and having ten men ordained as the country's first monks. By tradition the monk also founded Bulgapsa, a temple in Yeonggwang on Korea's southwest coast that still stands. The whole thing was diplomatic: Buddhism came bundled as a gift of friendship between two royal courts, not as missionaries preaching to crowds.

events.label: Gwanggaeto the Great
events.description: In just twenty-two years on the throne, the teenage king Gwanggaeto blasted Goguryeo outward in every direction — north into Manchuria, west onto the Liaodong Peninsula, south against Baekje and Japanese raiders — making it the dominant power in northeast Asia.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: His memorial stele brags that he took 64 walled towns and 1,400 villages, a tally so specific it reads like a victory ledger. His formal posthumous title was a mouthful even by royal standards: Gukgangsang Gwanggaeto-gyeong Pyeongan Hotaewang, usually shortened to "Gwanggaeto the Great." He was also the first Korean ruler we know of to declare his own era name (Yeongnak, "Eternal Rejoicing"), a bold move normally reserved for Chinese emperors — Goguryeo was announcing it answered to no one.

events.label: Baekje-Japan Cultural Exchange
events.description: Across the fourth through sixth centuries, Baekje fed early Japan a steady stream of writing, Confucian learning, technology, and eventually Buddhism — making it the cultural bridge from the mainland to the islands.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The pivotal handoff is dated to either 538 or 552, when Baekje's King Seong shipped Japan's court a gilt-bronze image of the Buddha, ritual banners, and sutras. The gift split Japan's elite down the middle: the pro-mainland Soga clan championed the new faith while the Mononobe clan, hereditary guardians of the native gods (kami), fought to keep it out — a feud that turned into open civil war before the Buddhists won. So the religion that became Japanese Zen and Pure Land arrived as a diplomatic package from a Korean king.

events.label: Silla Gold Crowns
events.description: Silla's royal tombs at Gyeongju held some of the most spectacular gold crowns in East Asian archaeology — sheet-gold headpieces sprouting tree-branch and antler shapes, hung with jade ornaments.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The tree and antler shapes aren't just decoration: scholars read the tree as a 'world tree' linking earth to heaven, and the antlers may nod to the reindeer of the Eurasian steppe far to the north, hinting at where Silla's ruling families traced their roots. The tombs that held these crowns get wonderfully literal names — one is Cheonmachong, the 'Heavenly Horse Tomb,' named for a painting found inside. And buried alongside the gold was proof of just how far Silla's trade reached: a blue glass cup chemically matched to Roman glassmaking, carried thousands of miles up the Silk Road through Central Asia and China to this corner of Korea.

events.label: Gwanggaeto Stele Erected
events.description: A year after Gwanggaeto's death, his son Jangsu raised a towering inscribed stone near the old capital to broadcast his father's conquests — at 6.4 meters (about 21 feet), it is the largest inscribed stele in East Asia and the single most important written source for early Korean history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The monument vanished into mud and overgrowth for centuries and was only rediscovered around 1875 by a Chinese epigrapher. When Japan's army obtained a rubbing in 1884, officers seized on one weathered passage about the year 391 to argue Japan had once ruled part of southern Korea — a reading Korean scholars fiercely dispute, and the inscription remains a political flashpoint among Korea, China, and Japan to this day. The stone carries 1,802 classical Chinese characters cut into all four faces.

events.label: Jangsu Moves Capital to Pyongyang
events.description: King Jangsu moved Goguryeo's capital south to Pyongyang, planting the kingdom in the fertile western plains and turning it from a mountain stronghold into a peninsula-wide power that loomed over Baekje and Silla.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Jangsu's name literally means "Long Life," and he earned it — he died in 491 at around 97 or 98 years old after a reign of nearly 79 years, one of the longest of any monarch in recorded world history. In 475 his armies stormed Baekje's capital Hanseong (modern Seoul) and executed King Gaero, a blow Baekje never undid. He was also a shrewd diplomat, sending tribute to BOTH rival Chinese courts at once so neither could lean on him.

events.label: Baekje Buddhist Art Flourishes
events.description: Baekje's sculptors and temple-builders turned out work so refined it set the template for early Japanese Buddhist art — and produced the gilt-bronze incense burner now considered a national treasure.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Baekje Gilt-bronze Incense Burner, dug up in 1993 from a temple site at Neungsan-ri in Buyeo, was Korea's National Treasure No. 287 and the standout among some 450 artifacts found there. It stands about 25 inches (64 cm) tall, weighs roughly 26 pounds (11.8 kg), and packs its lotus-shaped lid with mountain peaks, five tiny musicians, and sacred beasts under a phoenix, all balanced on a rearing dragon. The dragon-and-phoenix pairing reads as yin and yang — a Taoist idea riding on a Buddhist object, which is exactly the kind of blend Baekje art was known for.

events.label: Gyeongju Royal Tombs
events.description: Gyeongju is studded with more than 150 grassy burial mounds, some as tall as a six-story building, holding the gold crowns, glassware, and jade of Silla's royal dead. The largest cluster is the Daereungwon tomb park downtown.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Daereungwon park alone holds 23 of these mounds. The most famous, Cheonmachong ('Heavenly Horse Tomb'), was opened in 1973 and is about 12.7 meters high and 50 meters across; inside, archaeologists found a gold crown and a painted saddle flap showing a white horse in mid-gallop, the artwork that gave the tomb its name and one of the rare surviving Silla paintings. The biggest of all, Hwangnamdaechong, is a twin mound for a king and queen and gave up a separate gold crown and belt for the woman. Silla tombs were built mound-over-stone in a way that made them nearly impossible to rob, which is why so much gold survived intact.

events.label: Idu Writing System
events.description: Koreans devised idu, a workaround that bent Chinese characters to fit Korean grammar — using some characters for meaning and others purely for sound — so they could finally write their own language.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The system was famously regularized by Seol Chong, a Silla scholar and the son of the celebrated monk Wonhyo; though pieces of idu were already in use, he gave it consistent rules. It was one of a family of Chinese-character workarounds Koreans built, alongside hyangchal (used to write vernacular poetry) and gugyeol (reading aids scribbled into Chinese texts). Idu proved astonishingly durable for official documents, surviving into the era of the Joseon dynasty long after the Korean alphabet was invented.

events.label: Silla on the Silk Road
events.description: Glassware and gold filigree pulled from Gyeongju's tombs prove Silla was wired into trade routes reaching all the way to the Mediterranean. Roman and Middle Eastern objects crossed thousands of miles to be buried with Silla royals.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The standout find came from the Hwangnamdaechong twin mound, excavated in 1975: a glass ewer (pitcher) and three cups, identified as late-Roman work from around the fourth century and now grouped as National Treasure No. 193. Across the Silla tombs, archaeologists have logged roughly 30 imported glass vessels in all. Chemical testing complicates the simple 'Roman' label, since some pieces match Sasanian Persian glass rather than Mediterranean workshops, meaning these treasures likely changed hands many times along the Silk Road, across the Eurasian steppe and through Central Asia, before reaching the Korean coast.

events.label: Silla Bone Rank System
events.description: King Beopheung formalized the bone-rank system, a hereditary caste ladder so rigid it dictated not just who could hold office but the size of your house, the color of your clothes, and whom you could marry.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The top of the ladder, the 'sacred bone' (seonggol) rank reserved for kings, was so exclusive that the bloodline eventually ran out — and when there were no sacred-bone men left, Silla turned to sacred-bone women, crowning Queen Seondeok in 632, one of the very few reigning queens in East Asian history. The same King Beopheung who locked in this hierarchy also gambled on Buddhism: in 527 his courtier Ichadon volunteered to be executed to force the issue, prophesying that milk, not blood, would flow from his neck. The legend says it did, and a shaken aristocracy let the king make Buddhism official.

events.label: Buddhism Adopted in Silla
events.description: Silla adopted Buddhism in 527 only after the young courtier Ichadon staged his own execution to force the issue — and, the legend says, milk-white blood sprayed from his neck.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ichadon was only about 26 (born 501, executed 527), and the story goes that he engineered his own death on purpose: when the king balked at killing him, Ichadon deliberately provoked the anti-Buddhist ministers into demanding it. The execution fell on the 15th day of the 9th lunar month, and his death made him the convert who finally cracked the aristocracy's resistance. His martyrdom paid for Heungnyunsa, Silla's first state-sponsored temple. The peninsula's most isolated kingdom thus became Buddhist a century and a half after Goguryeo and Baekje.

events.label: Hwarang Warrior Corps
events.description: Silla's 'Flower Knights' were an elite corps of young noblemen drilled in war and the arts alike, a finishing school for the generals and statesmen who would carry the kingdom to the top of the peninsula.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The corps actually grew out of a scrapped earlier experiment, the Wonhwa ('original flowers'), two bands of young women that fell apart after one leader murdered her rival out of jealousy; the king then re-launched the idea with handpicked boys. The famous five precepts (loyalty, filial piety, trust, never retreat, never kill without cause) weren't an internal rule book but advice the warriors sought from a Buddhist monk named Won Gwang, known as the Sesok Ogye, the 'five worldly commandments.' Sources even disagree on when the Hwarang began, with dates ranging from 540 to 576.

events.label: Hwangnyongsa Temple Built
events.description: Silla built the massive Hwangnyongsa temple complex in Gyeongju, featuring a legendary nine-story wooden pagoda nearly 80 meters (260 feet) tall — one of the tallest structures in East Asia at the time. The temple stood for nearly 700 years before Mongol invaders destroyed it in 1238.

events.label: Silla Conquers Gaya
events.description: Silla swallowed the last independent Gaya states, absorbing their iron mines, master metalworkers, and sea-trade links — and removing the buffer that had separated Silla from Baekje.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The conquest came in stages: the leading state, Geumgwan Gaya, surrendered to Silla back in 532, and the final holdout, Daegaya, centered at Goryeong, fell in 562. King Jinheung's campaign was famously carried out by his general Isabu, with a teenage warrior of the elite Hwarang corps named Sadaham distinguishing himself in the assault. Folding in Gaya's iron-working heartland gave Silla exactly the economic and military muscle it would soon throw against Baekje and Goguryeo in the unification wars.

events.label: Early Korean Histories Compiled
events.description: By the sixth and early seventh centuries, all three kingdoms were writing down their own official histories — proof they now saw themselves as literate states with stories worth preserving.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Goguryeo's Sinjip (600) was actually a slimmed-down five-volume edit of a much older hundred-volume chronicle called the Yugi. Baekje's history, the Seogi, had been compiled even earlier, by the scholar Goheung around 375 under King Geunchogo. Silla's National History was assembled in 545 by the general-scholar Geochilbu, who pulled together a team of literati on royal command. Not a single original page of any of the three survives — everything we have is quoted secondhand in the Samguk Sagi, written some six centuries later in 1145.

events.label: Mireuksa Temple Built
events.description: Around 602, Baekje raised Mireuksa, the largest Buddhist temple the country ever built, anchored by a colossal stone pagoda (a tower built as a shrine) that still partly stands.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: A gold plaque found inside in 2009 records that the pagoda was commissioned in 639 by a queen of King Mu, who reigned 600–640. The surviving west pagoda was about 47 feet (14.2 m) tall when it was taken apart and is reckoned to have originally risen nine stories. South Korea spent roughly two decades dismantling and rebuilding it stone by stone, finally unveiling the restored pagoda to the public in 2019. The temple sits not at the old capital but in modern Iksan, and the whole site is now a UNESCO World Heritage listing.

events.label: General Eulji Mundeok
events.description: Goguryeo's most famous general baited a vastly larger Sui army into chasing him into hostile country, wore it down, and then annihilated it at the Salsu River — capping the trick by sending the enemy commander a taunting poem first.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: That four-line poem to Sui general Yu Zhongwen — which sneered that he'd won enough glory and should quit while ahead — is celebrated as the oldest surviving piece of written Korean literature. Strangely, almost nothing else about Eulji Mundeok's life is recorded; outside this one campaign he is nearly a blank. His legend looms so large that South Korea and the United States named a major annual military exercise ("Ulchi") after him.

events.label: Goguryeo Defeats Sui China
events.description: When Sui China hurled an enormous army at Goguryeo in 612, General Eulji Mundeok let it march deep and hungry, then shattered the retreating force at the Salsu River — a catastrophe so total it helped topple the Sui dynasty itself.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Chinese records put the full invasion force at over a million men, with a 305,000-strong spearhead sent to take Pyongyang; supposedly fewer than 2,700 of that spearhead made it home. The dramatic broken-dam flood is a later tradition — no contemporary source mentions it — but the lopsided slaughter is well attested. The defeat broke Emperor Yang of Sui: rebellions fed by the war's ruinous cost spread across China, and within six years the dynasty was gone, replaced by the Tang.

events.label: Queen Seondeok of Silla
events.description: Silla's 27th ruler and Korea's first reigning queen, Seondeok poured the kingdom's resources into Buddhism and learning while fending off Goguryeo and Baekje, setting up the diplomatic gamble that would unify Korea.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Her great building project was the nine-story wooden pagoda at Hwangnyongsa (the 'Imperial Dragon Temple'), begun around 634 and reckoned the tallest structure in East Asia at the time; each story was meant to ward off a different hostile neighbor. The pagoda burned during the Mongol invasions of the 1200s and was never rebuilt, so only the stone foundations survive today. Her observatory, Cheomseongdae, was built early in her reign partly to read the skies for farmers, tying royal prestige to the harvest.

events.label: Yeon Gaesomun Seizes Power
events.description: Goguryeo's hardline general Yeon Gaesomun staged a bloody coup, slaughtering the king and roughly a hundred ministers and ruling the kingdom as a military dictator behind a puppet on the throne.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The trap was almost theatrical: Yeon Gaesomun threw a lavish banquet to mark his promotion to a regional governorship, invited the rival ministers, and had his troops kill all hundred or so of them on the spot. He then had King Yeongnyu killed (older accounts say his body was dismembered and tossed aside) and installed the king's nephew Bojang as a figurehead, taking for himself the title Dae Mangniji, the highest office Goguryeo had. The split he won by force was real: Goguryeo's court had been divided between an appeasement faction that wanted to stay on Tang China's good side and the war-hawks Yeon led.

events.label: Goguryeo-Tang Wars
events.description: Goguryeo did to Tang China what it had done to the Sui: it broke the great conqueror Emperor Taizong against a single fortress, Ansi, which held for nearly three months in 645 and forced the most powerful ruler in Asia to turn back.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Taizong put around 5,000 laborers to work for sixty days building a giant earthen ramp to top the walls — but the mound collapsed, and the defenders charged out and seized it for themselves. Goguryeo records are so thin that the fortress commander's name doesn't even appear in early sources; later Korean writers call him Yang Manchun and add the relished (and unverifiable) legend that he shot an arrow into Taizong's eye. Tang would only finish Goguryeo decades later, and only by abandoning the frontal assault and attacking from the south alongside Silla.

events.label: Cheomseongdae Observatory
events.description: Built under Queen Seondeok, this bottle-shaped stone tower in Gyeongju is the oldest surviving astronomical observatory in East Asia, its very design a calendar in granite.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The numbers are deliberate: its 362 stones stand for the days of the lunar year, its 27 stacked layers mark Seondeok as Silla's 27th monarch, and the small square window has exactly 12 courses of stone above and below it for the 12 months. The window faces south and is positioned so sunlight strikes the interior floor at the equinoxes, making the tower itself a seasonal clock. It still stands intact in Gyeongju as part of a UNESCO World Heritage site, having outlasted the kingdom that built it by more than a thousand years.

events.label: General Kim Yu-sin
events.description: Silla's greatest general and the strategic brain behind unification, Kim Yusin commanded the armies that crushed Baekje and Goguryeo despite being born an outsider, into conquered Gaya royalty.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He joined the Hwarang youth corps at fifteen, leading a band nicknamed Yonghwa-hyangdo. He locked himself into the heart of Silla's power not just by winning battles but by marriage: his sister married the future king Muyeol, and Kim Yusin in turn married into the royal house, so the conquests were a family enterprise. He lived to 79, dying on the first day of the seventh lunar month in 673, and was so revered that the throne later granted him the posthumous title of King Heungmu, an honor essentially never given to a man who was never king.

events.label: Fall of Baekje
events.description: A two-pronged Silla-Tang assault wiped out Baekje in a single summer, breaking the southwestern kingdom after nearly seven centuries and ending with the mass suicide of its court at the Rock of the Falling Flowers.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Baekje's last stand came at Hwangsanbeol (near modern Nonsan), where General Gyebaek, having reportedly killed his own wife and children so they could never be enslaved, threw 5,000 men against Kim Yusin's 50,000 and beat back the Silla attack five times before being overwhelmed. The battle turned on a teenage Hwarang named Gwanchang, who charged the Baekje lines alone; Gyebaek spared him once out of respect for his youth, but when the boy attacked again he was beheaded and his body sent back, which shamed and enraged the wavering Silla troops into a final push. Baekje had spent generations exporting Buddhism, art, and writing to Japan, which is why Japan would soon try to save it.

events.label: Monk Wonhyo
events.description: Wonhyo was Korea's most influential Buddhist philosopher, famous for an enlightenment in a tomb (he gulped delicious water in the dark, then recoiled at dawn to find it was rainwater in a human skull) and for taking Buddhism out of the monasteries and into the streets for ordinary people.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: His name means 'Dawnbreak,' and he was astonishingly prolific, with his writings running to more than 80 works in some 240 volumes, more than any other figure in Korean Buddhist history. His signature idea was hwajaeng, the 'harmonization of disputes,' an attempt to reconcile Buddhism's many feuding schools by showing they pointed to one underlying truth. He broke his vows and married, and his son Seol Chong grew up to become one of Silla's great Confucian scholars, credited with helping systematize the idu writing system used to render Korean with Chinese characters.

events.label: Fall of Goguryeo
events.description: The toughest of the Three Kingdoms finally fell in 668, undone not by Tang's armies but by a family feud at the top that handed China the keys.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: When the dictator Yeon Gaesomun died in 666, his three sons turned on each other; the eldest, Yeon Namsaeng, defected to Tang and personally guided the invasion of his own homeland. The Tang general Li Ji crossed the Yalu River and besieged Pyongyang alongside Silla forces in the autumn of 668. The end was treachery all the way down: with the youngest brother Yeon Namgeon still holding out in the inner city, his own general, a Buddhist monk named Sin Seong, opened the gates to the enemy.

events.label: Silla Unifies Korea
events.description: With both rivals destroyed, Silla immediately turned on its Tang ally, launching a seven-year war (670 to 676) to throw China off the peninsula rather than become a Chinese province.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Tang had never planned to leave: it carved the conquered lands into Chinese-run zones, including the Andong Protectorate over former Goguryeo, and treated the whole peninsula as imperial territory. Silla's counter-move was guerrilla in spirit, arming and backing Baekje and Goguryeo resistance fighters against their new Chinese overlords and absorbing the survivors into its own ranks. The resulting state, often called Unified or Later Silla, would run from 668 all the way to 935, the longest single grip any kingdom held over Korea up to that point.

events.label: Silla Expels Tang Forces
events.description: Silla's underdog war against the world's strongest empire ended in victory: a string of battles drove Tang north of the Taedong River and won Korean rule over Korea for good.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The hinge was the clash at Maeso Fortress (modern Yeoncheon) on September 29, 675, where a Silla force of about 30,000 under Kim Wonsul reportedly faced a vastly larger Tang army and held, halting China's advance. The naval defeat of Tang at Gibeolpo near the Geum River estuary the following year sealed it. Notably, the same Kim Wonsul who anchored the war's pivotal battle was the son of the great Kim Yusin, who had died only two years earlier, so the unification really was a multi-generation family campaign.

events.label: Silla National Confucian Academy
events.description: In 682 Unified Silla founded the Gukhak (National Academy), a state school that drilled future officials in the Confucian classics and Chinese-style administration. It nudged the kingdom toward hiring on merit, though the hereditary bone-rank system still held the real power.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: It opened in 682, the second year of King Sinmun, and was Silla's only recorded institution of higher learning. A bigger step came in 788, when the court added a graded reading examination that ranked candidates by how well they had mastered Confucian texts, an early echo of China's civil-service exams. But the meritocracy had a ceiling built in: under the bone-rank rules, your birth still capped how high you could rise no matter how well you scored, so the exam never broke the aristocracy's grip the way it eventually would in later Korean dynasties.

events.label: Unified Silla Golden Age
events.description: After unifying the peninsula, Silla settled into a golden age of Buddhist art, Confucian scholarship, and long-distance trade, all radiating from the capital at Gyeongju. Boosters claimed the city held nearly a million people; the truth was smaller but still made it one of Asia's great cities.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The thirteenth-century Samguk Yusa records Gyeongju at its peak as having 178,936 households spread across 1,360 districts and 55 avenues, with 35 separate palaces, the household figure being the source of the inflated 'one million' claim. Its fame traveled far: the ninth-century Arab geographer Ibn Khordadbeh described Silla in 'The Book of Roads and Kingdoms,' telling readers as far away as Persia of a wealthy land beyond China. The era's stability rested on the reigns of King Sinmun (who consolidated the new state) and King Seongdeok, whose long rule is often counted as the high-water mark.

events.label: Hyangga Poetry Tradition
events.description: Silla poets wrote hyangga ('native songs'), the oldest Korean-language poetry, using a system called hyangchal that pressed Chinese characters into service to spell out Korean sounds and grammar. Their themes ran to Buddhist devotion, longing, love, and grief.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Only 25 survive, but they come from two sources, not one: 14 are preserved in the thirteenth-century Samguk Yusa and the other 11 in the Gyunyeojeon, a biography of the monk Gyunyeo. Roughly eighteen of the surviving poems carry Buddhist themes. The best known, the Cheoyongga ('Song of Cheoyong'), tells of a man who comes home to find a plague spirit with his wife and, instead of raging, sings and dances in forgiveness, so disarming the spirit that it flees; the song became a folk charm sung to ward off disease.

events.label: Unified Silla Stoneware
events.description: Unified Silla potters made hard, high-fired gray stoneware decorated with stamped patterns of flowers and geometric shapes. This work laid the technical groundwork for the celadon (jade-green glazed ware) that would later make Korea world-famous.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Buddhism reshaped the craft: as cremation replaced burial, potters shifted to making stamped funerary urns to hold ashes, often deposited at temples or sealed inside pagodas. The real bridge to celadon was a technical breakthrough in the eighth century, the first deliberate ash glaze, a rudimentary green coating that would mature into Goryeo celadon. One excavated Silla urn was even capped with an imported celadon bowl from China's Yuezhou kilns, hard evidence that Silla potters were studying the advanced Tang ceramics they would eventually rival.

events.label: Bulguksa Temple Built
events.description: Chief minister Kim Daeseong commissioned Bulguksa ('Temple of the Buddha Land') on a hillside outside Gyeongju, a Unified Silla masterpiece of stone terraces, ornamental bridges, and twin stone pagodas. Its eighth-century granite foundations and pagodas are original; the wooden halls were rebuilt after war and fire.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Kim Daeseong died before the temple was finished, so the Silla royal court completed it in 774, more than two decades after the 751 start. The two pagodas are wildly mismatched on purpose: the plain three-story Seokgatap stands 8.2 meters tall (about 27 feet) while the ornate, almost lacy Dabotap rises to 10.4 meters (about 34 feet), and both are designated National Treasures of Korea. The temple was gutted during the Japanese invasions of 1592 to 1598, when the wooden buildings burned and never fully recovered until twentieth-century restoration.

events.label: Mugujeonggwang Great Dharani Sutra
events.description: The Mugujeonggwang Great Dharani Sutra, a Buddhist prayer scroll printed from carved woodblocks, is the oldest surviving woodblock-printed document on Earth. It was discovered in 1966 sealed inside Bulguksa's Seokgatap pagoda.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Workers found it on October 13, 1966, during repairs to the pagoda, tucked in with other relics; the scroll is a string of twelve sheets of mulberry-bark paper, brittle and damaged after twelve centuries inside the stone. Scholars date it between 704 and 751: the underlying text was translated from Sanskrit into Chinese in 704, and the pagoda itself was finished by 751, so the print can be no later than that. That window puts it more than a century ahead of China's dated Diamond Sutra of 868, which had long been called the world's oldest printed book.

events.label: Seokguram Grotto
events.description: On a ridge above Bulguksa, builders fitted hundreds of granite blocks into an artificial cave and buried it under earth, then placed a serene seated Buddha inside facing the sunrise over the East Sea. The mortarless domed ceiling is an eighth-century engineering marvel.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The main Buddha is about 3.5 meters tall (roughly 11.5 feet) and sits on a lotus pedestal another 1.34 meters high, all carved from white granite. The domed rotunda is roughly 7.2 meters across and uses a corbelled ceiling, where each ring of stone steps slightly inward over the one below until they close at the top, capped by a single lotus-carved stone weighing about 20 tons. The whole structure runs about 14 meters deep from the entrance through a connecting corridor to the rear wall, and the original design let air circulate so condensation never fogged the figure, a passive system that twentieth-century concrete repairs actually disrupted.

events.label: Emille Bell Cast
events.description: The Divine Bell of King Seongdeok, nicknamed the Emille Bell, is a colossal bronze bell cast in 771 and covered in relief carvings of lotuses and flying apsaras (Buddhist celestial spirits). Its deep, eerie tone inspired a grim legend about a child cast into the molten metal.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: A precise 1997 weighing pegged it at 18.9 tons, and it stands 3.75 meters tall (about 12 feet) with walls 12 to 25 centimeters thick. King Gyeongdeok began the project to honor his late father Seongdeok, but it took so long that it was finished under his grandson, King Hyegong, in late 771. Korea made it National Treasure No. 29 in 1962. Tellingly, the child-sacrifice legend appears in no record before the twentieth century, surfacing only during the Japanese colonial period, which is why historians treat it as folklore invented to explain the haunting sound rather than history.

events.label: Jang Bogo's Maritime Empire
events.description: Born a commoner, Jang Bogo built a maritime empire from Cheonghaejin, a fortified naval base on Wando Island off Silla's southwest coast. He swept pirates from the Yellow Sea and dominated the sea lanes linking Korea, China, and Japan before rivals had him killed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He won King Heungdeok's blessing to build the garrison in 828 and is said to have trained 10,000 men there. His reach extended into China, where he founded a Korean temple in Shandong and bankrolled the long pilgrimage of the Japanese monk Ennin, whose travel diary is a prime eyewitness source on the era. His downfall was ambition: when he pushed to marry his daughter into the royal house, the bone-rank aristocracy balked at a commoner's blood entering the line, and in 846 a court agent named Yeomjang gained his trust, then killed him with a knife hidden in his clothes.

events.label: Later Three Kingdoms Period
events.description: As Silla's central government rotted, two warlords broke off their own kingdoms and a shrunken Silla clung to its southeast corner, reviving the old three-way split of the peninsula. This Later Three Kingdoms period set up the final contest to reunify Korea.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: In 892 the strongman Gyeon Hwon carved out a state in the southwest and in 900 formally named it Later Baekje, claiming to restore the long-dead kingdom of that name. In 901 a Buddhist-monk-turned-warlord, Gung Ye, founded a rival northern state he called Later Goguryeo, later renaming it twice (Majin, then Taebong) and moving his capital from Songak to Cheorwon. Gung Ye's reign curdled into terror: he proclaimed himself the Maitreya, the future Buddha, claimed he could read minds, and executed officials for imagined treason, behavior that would soon get him overthrown.

events.label: Wang Geon Founds Goryeo
events.description: Wang Geon, a merchant's son from the trading city of Kaesong, overthrew the increasingly mad warlord Gung Ye in 918 and founded the Goryeo dynasty, the kingdom that gave 'Korea' its English name. He combined armies with alliances to reunify the peninsula.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: His marriage diplomacy was extraordinary even by the standards of the age: he took a reported 29 wives, most of them daughters of regional power-holders, knitting their families to his throne and leaving him with dozens of children, an arrangement that later bred deadly succession fights. Near the end of his life he left his heirs the 'Ten Injunctions,' a set of rules warning against northern nomads, urging support for Buddhism, and cautioning about rivalry within the royal clan. Reigning as Taejo until 943, he finished the reunification in 936.

events.label: Silla Surrenders to Goryeo
events.description: In 935 the last Silla king, Gyeongsun, peacefully handed his throne to Wang Geon rather than fight, ending a dynasty that had lasted nearly a thousand years. Wang Geon treated him generously, easing the transition to Goryeo rule.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Gyeongsun ruled only a tiny remnant around Gyeongju before deciding surrender would spare his people and aristocracy; tradition says he led a procession of officials and treasure to Wang Geon's capital stretching for miles. Wang Geon married his own eldest daughter, Princess Nangrang, to the deposed king and appointed Gyeongsun governor of Gyeongju, making him the first holder of Goryeo's new sasim-gwan (regional inspector) post. The marriage ran both ways, binding the old and new royal lines together, a textbook example of how Wang Geon absorbed former rulers rather than crushing them.
